explanations.answer: The whole supply of food and water
explanations.explanation: That's exactly the list. Isaiah says the Lord GOD of Hosts is about to remove "both supply and support: the whole supply of food and water" (Isaiah 3:1). Food and water, friend. No pantry in the world is ready for that, and I own a LOT of ovens.

explanations.answer: All the gold in the treasury
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, gold sounds like what a city would lose. But the verse names something more basic: "the whole supply of food and water" (Isaiah 3:1). Gold is nice to have, but you can't eat it, and you can't drink it either.

Horses and chariots feel like big-city stuff, I know. But they're not on this list. The verse says the Lord is removing "the whole supply of food and water" (Isaiah 3:1). Nobody ever got through a long day on chariot power alone.

Right on the money, friend. After food and water, the list turns to people: the judge, the prophet, the elder, the counselor and more (Isaiah 3:2-3). It's the people folks look to when things get shaky. Take them away and everybody's looking around going, "Who's in charge?"

Food does come up, but farmers and shepherds aren't named. The list runs through the mighty man, the warrior, the judge, the prophet and the elder, plus the commander of fifty and the counselor (Isaiah 3:2-3). Those are the folks people turn to for direction. Not a shepherd in the bunch.

Good guess, but builders and craftsmen don't show up here. The verses name people like the judge, the prophet, the elder and the counselor (Isaiah 3:2-3). It's a list of leaders and advisers. Not one hammer in sight.

I see why you'd think so, since the leaders are gone and somebody has to step in. But that's not what the text says. The next line is God speaking: "I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them." (Isaiah 3:4). No foreign kings anywhere in that sentence.

That's right, friend. No kings from other nations are mentioned. The text says, "I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them." (Isaiah 3:4). The replacements are lads and children.

That's it. Isaiah says, "The people will oppress one another, man against man, neighbor against neighbor" (Isaiah 3:5). It's not an army from outside doing it. It's people turning on the folks right next to them. I think that's a hard thing to read.

explanations.answer: They will share what they have
explanations.explanation: I wish that's how it went, I really do. But the verse says the opposite: "The people will oppress one another, man against man, neighbor against neighbor" (Isaiah 3:5). Sharing is nowhere in this picture. It's a heavy one.

explanations.answer: They will stay out of each other's way
explanations.explanation: Keeping to yourself sounds peaceful, but that's not the picture. Isaiah says "The people will oppress one another, man against man, neighbor against neighbor" (Isaiah 3:5). They're not avoiding each other, they're going at each other. Even the young will rise up against the old.

Rubble is the word. The man says, "Take charge of this heap of rubble." (Isaiah 3:6). Think about that job posting for a second. Come on in, we've got a heap of rubble and a cloak, and the cloak is YOURS!

Gold would've been a tempting promotion, wouldn't it? But the verse says the man tells his brother, "Take charge of this heap of rubble." (Isaiah 3:6). Nobody's handing out treasure here, friend. It's a pile of broken pieces.

Grain would at least be useful, since food has already been taken away. But the man's words are, "Take charge of this heap of rubble." (Isaiah 3:6). A heap of rubble, and that's the whole job. I'd ask about the benefits package too.

That's right. On that day the man cries aloud, "Do not make me leader of the people!" (Isaiah 3:7). He says he's no healer and has no food or clothing in his house. I think he knows exactly how big this mess is, and he wants no part of it.

He actually says no, and loudly. The man cries aloud, "I am not a healer. I have no food or clothing in my house. Do not make me leader of the people!" (Isaiah 3:7). Somebody grabbed him by the cloak and he is NOT having it.

explanations.answer: They spoke and acted against the LORD
explanations.explanation: There it is. Isaiah says, "Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen because they spoke and acted against the LORD, defying His glorious presence." (Isaiah 3:8). Words and actions both. The reason is given right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: Their armies were too small to win
explanations.explanation: Armies are what you'd expect a city to blame, I get it. But Isaiah gives a different reason: "because they spoke and acted against the LORD, defying His glorious presence." (Isaiah 3:8). The verse never mentions the size of any army.

explanations.answer: Their walls were not strong enough
explanations.explanation: Walls are a fair guess, friend, but they're never brought up. Isaiah says, "Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen because they spoke and acted against the LORD" (Isaiah 3:8). The cause is how they spoke and acted toward the LORD. Stone had nothing to do with it.

I see why that sounds reasonable, since most of us try to hide our mess. But Isaiah says the opposite: "they flaunt their sin; they do not conceal it." (Isaiah 3:9). No hard work at hiding anything here. It's out in the open.

That's right. Isaiah says, "like Sodom they flaunt their sin; they do not conceal it." (Isaiah 3:9). Sodom was a city known for its sin (Genesis 19). I've dropped a whole tray of cookies and tried to hide it, so this level of not hiding is something else.

explanations.answer: It will be well with them
explanations.explanation: Yes, and it's good news in the middle of a heavy chapter. Isaiah says, "Tell the righteous it will be well with them, for they will enjoy the fruit of their labor." (Isaiah 3:10). A word of hope for the righteous. Don't skip over it.

Running away is what a lot of us would expect, but the verse doesn't say that. The message is, "Tell the righteous it will be well with them" (Isaiah 3:10). The righteous hear that it will be well. Nobody's packing a bag.

explanations.answer: They will fall with the rest
explanations.explanation: After all that stumbling and falling, I see why you'd go there. But the message for the righteous is different: "it will be well with them, for they will enjoy the fruit of their labor." (Isaiah 3:10). Good news is waiting for them.

That's the one. Isaiah says, "they will be repaid with what their hands have done." (Isaiah 3:11). The righteous enjoy the fruit of their labor, and the wicked get repaid for their own doing. Each one gets what their own hands made.
Fathers make a tempting answer, but the verse brings them up nowhere. It says, "they will be repaid with what their hands have done." (Isaiah 3:11). It's their own hands, their own doing.

Enemies are an easy thing to blame, friend. But Isaiah doesn't mention them here. He says, "they will be repaid with what their hands have done." (Isaiah 3:11). The repayment comes from their own hands.

That's right. God says, "Youths oppress My people, and women rule over them." (Isaiah 3:12). It matches the earlier line about lads as leaders (Isaiah 3:4). And notice He calls them "My people." They belong to Him.

Kings are what you'd expect when people are being oppressed. But this verse names someone else: "Youths oppress My people, and women rule over them." (Isaiah 3:12). It's youths in the verse. Nobody mentions a king.

Priests are a natural guess, since they're leaders too. But this verse doesn't name them. God says, "Youths oppress My people, and women rule over them." (Isaiah 3:12). The word in the verse is youths.

Yes, and it's God Himself saying it. "O My people, your guides mislead you; they turn you from your paths." (Isaiah 3:12). The ones meant to point the way are steering people off course. I once followed a recipe card that skipped the sugar, so I know what that feels like, and it wasn't this serious.

It's true, friend. God says, "O My people, your guides mislead you; they turn you from your paths." (Isaiah 3:12). The guides are the problem. And He still calls them "My people," which I think says a lot.

explanations.answer: The elders and leaders of His people
explanations.explanation: That's right. "The LORD brings this charge against the elders and leaders of His people" (Isaiah 3:14). Nothing here is hidden. The charge goes straight to the ones in charge.

explanations.answer: The kings of the nations around Judah
explanations.explanation: Other kings are a reasonable guess, but they aren't named. The verse says, "The LORD brings this charge against the elders and leaders of His people" (Isaiah 3:14). It's about His own people's leaders. Foreign kings don't show up.

explanations.answer: The priests who serve in the temple
explanations.explanation: Priests feel close, but they're not named in this charge. The verse says, "The LORD brings this charge against the elders and leaders of His people" (Isaiah 3:14). Elders and leaders are who the charge lands on.

Yes, the poor. The LORD says, "You have devoured the vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses." (Isaiah 3:14). It's a heavy charge. I think this one hurts to read, and the next verse asks why they crush His people.

Nations sound like what you'd plunder, I know. But the LORD says, "the plunder of the poor is in your houses." (Isaiah 3:14). It's the poor of His own people, not other nations. That's what makes the charge so serious.

Temple is a guess I understand, since it's the most valuable place around. But the LORD says, "the plunder of the poor is in your houses." (Isaiah 3:14). What they're holding is the poor's plunder. The temple isn't part of this charge.
